extracted.intended_audience: literary readers, critics, and writers (readers of literary reviews)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and critiquing an author's prose and poetry (style, argument, narration, moral tone, and use of evidence), with attention to how form suits subject and how reasoning is marshalled in political/economic passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincing argumentation when making charges
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author raises a charge (e.g., calling someone a 'scoundrel' or 'blockhead'), it ought to be met with something more convincing than mere epithets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on insults or rhetorical bravado; supply reasons and evidence rather than name-calling. The text castigates unsupported personal invective as inadequate justification for serious claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical coherence and rigor in political and prose argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Political instruction or moral/political argument must be founded on logical reasoning and evidence rather than on poetical creation or feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat political systems as 'mere day-dreams' or rely on grand imaginative vision when precision and logic are required. The reviewer faults Mr. Southey for letting poetic temperament override analytical accuracy; writers should provide consistent principles and factual support when arguing politics or history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional probability and internal plausibility in imaginative works
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of art should not continually violate conventional probability; even extravagant visions require a measure of plausibility to be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grotesque or extravagant inventions (e.g., gorgeous but implausible visions) must still respect enough internal or conventional probability to preserve artistic effect; otherwise they become merely absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of form to task: narration vs. argument
rubrics_metrics.description: An author’s strengths should be matched to the demands of the task—narrative constraints can improve writers who are better at 'filling up' than 'designing', while argumentative history requires a 'logical head'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing biography or history, adherence to the real course of events can restrain a writer’s inventive excesses; conversely, poets weak in systematic reasoning should avoid ambitious philosophical or political prose without adequate study and method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and plotting (plan of fictitious narratives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictitious narratives require felicitous design and planning; poor overall plan undermines even beautiful details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if there are 'innumerable beauties of detail', failure in original plan or plot can make narratives unsuccessful; strive for a coherent, well-conceived structure before ornamenting with detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and discernment in moral judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments of characters and actions must be rigorous but accompanied by discernment; avoid monkish austerity that flattens human complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid applying a uniform severe moral standard without nuance; recognize intermediate states and varieties of motive. The critic faults Southey for lacking discernment and treating people in extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic depiction of love and human feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals of love should show variety and plausibility rather than only Platonic abstraction or brute appetite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid flat extremes where lovers are 'either Seraphim or cattle'. Show gradations, earthly tenderness (e.g., paternal/filial tenderness), and human sympathy to make love scenes convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and use of humour (avoidance of forced jesting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour should not be quaintly or flippantly dull; forced jokes that would be ungenerous in print ought to be removed during revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit out jokes that are merely odd or petty (examples: teasing remarks about names like 'Bugg'); a writer should not publish every household jibe—proofing and self-restraint are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of rancour and excessive bitterness toward opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: A charitable and measured tone toward intellectual opponents is preferable to extraordinary bitterness; vitriol detracts from literary credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bitterness often arises from temperament and taste differences, but authors should aim to temper rigour with discernment and avoid hostile excess that suggests personal animus rather than principled critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of rhetorical machinery to subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary devices and plot machinery (e.g., ghosts, supernatural interlocutors) must serve a clear purpose and yield fresh insight rather than being contrived ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evoke a spirit merely to have it discuss mundane topics; machinery should reveal something new or appropriate. Gratuitous or ridiculous uses (ghost discussing periodicals) weaken effect and invite parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence and factual support in political/economic argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Political and economic claims require empirical support—statistical returns and comparative data—not picturesque impressions or aesthetic comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide facts (e.g., poor-rate statistics, mortality tables) and analyze them; avoid basing policy judgments on visual prettiness of cottages vs factories or on anecdotal hillside observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding fallacious analogies and bad illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies and metaphors used to explain economic or social principles must be sound; poor or fanciful comparisons (e.g., evaporation and dew) undermine argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test analogies for logical fit and explanatory power; do not substitute poetic simile for rigorous demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and coherence in political positions over time
rubrics_metrics.description: A public intellectual should avoid contradictory commitments (e.g., republicanism while opposing Catholic claims; desiring tyranny but abhorring office corruption) or else explain and reconcile them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when elements of a creed are logically linked; abandoning parts of a system without accounting for consequences invites critique that the positions are incoherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of limits of authorial competence (study before pronouncement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should not pronounce with authority on technical subjects (e.g., political economy) when they admit ignorance; rigorous study is required before public lecturing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one confesses lack of aptitude for a field, one should refrain from authoritative essays in it or else undertake the necessary empirical and theoretical work to avoid 'extraordinary blunders'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and language: the redeeming power of good prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty and purity of language can partially redeem weak reasoning or absurd ideas; prose style matters for reader engagement and can carry otherwise poor content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate clarity, purity, and charm in English; good stylistic gifts may make readers tolerate some weaknesses, though they are not a substitute for sound argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing utility of public works by private incentives and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical tests (private investment motive; tolls collected) are better indicators of the utility of public works than rhetorical assertion of 'national improvement'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether private speculators would invest (profit motive) or whether the public will pay for use (tolls); beware that ostentatious public works may be favored for fame rather than utility and are vulnerable to jobbing or corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding sweeping generalisation from aesthetic observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer the moral or political health of a population from the prettiness or ugliness of individual buildings or landscapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons such as 'cottage prettiness vs factory ugliness' are an inadequate method for assessing social or economic systems; use statistical and social evidence instead of purely picturesque judgment.
